events.author: oNP35iOMiLYO5lq_k4jZBdzLvsqAGATI0bZ1R8TqlEQ
events.body:
I actually think your integrity pin gives you a nice architectural boundary. The important principle is:

A pull request is not part of the repository until a trusted maintainer accepts it.

If that’s true, then nothing about creating or discussing a PR should ever affect the repository’s integrity pin.

Separate the repository from the inbox

Instead of thinking of PRs as “temporary Git branches,” think of them as messages addressed to a repository.

Repository
-----------
Git objects
Refs
Integrity PIN
Pull Request Inbox
------------------
PR metadata
Patch/branch reference
Comments
Reviews
Attachments
Signatures

The inbox is replicated.

The repository is not.

Until the maintainer merges the PR, the repository hasn’t changed, so the integrity PIN remains valid.

⸻

Don’t write to the repository itself

If you create commits on a hidden branch like:

refs/forkmesh/pr/*

you’ve technically modified the repository.

That raises awkward questions:

* Does the integrity PIN include hidden refs?
* Does git fsck see them?
* Do mirrors have to pin those objects?
* Can an attacker fill the object database with junk?

I’d avoid that.

⸻

Treat the PR inbox as append-only

Instead, imagine every mirror has something like:

repo.git
repo.inbox/

Inside repo.inbox:

pr-481/
    manifest.json
    comments/
    reviews/
    signatures/
    patches/

Every file is immutable and signed.

The mirrors replicate this directory.

When the source mirror comes back online, it downloads everything it missed.

⸻

Or make the inbox content-addressed

Even better, don’t use mutable folders.

Instead:

objects/
A1F9...
7C11...
9DAB...

Each object is signed.

Example:

PR Created
id: 481
base commit:
abc123
head:
def456
author:
Alice
signature:
...

Comments are separate objects.

Reviews are separate objects.

Approvals are separate objects.

Nothing is ever edited.

Only appended.

This becomes incredibly easy to replicate.

⸻

Integrity PIN never changes

The repository PIN should only cover:

Git commits
Trees
Blobs
Refs

Never:

PRs
Comments
Reviews
Labels
Reactions

Those are collaboration artifacts.

They’re not repository state.

⸻

Promotion is the only trusted operation

When the maintainer reconnects:

Inbox
PR
 |
 |
 v
Maintainer verifies
↓
Merge
↓
Repository changes
↓
New integrity PIN

The repository changes exactly once:

when the maintainer accepts the PR.

⸻

An idea I really like

One thing I think ForkMesh could do that GitHub can’t is make the inbox itself cryptographically verifiable.

For example:

Repository PIN
    ↓
Inbox Root Hash
    ↓
PR 481 hash
PR 482 hash
PR 483 hash

The mirrors periodically sign:

“As of timestamp T, the inbox consists of these 1,284 signed objects.”

Now mirrors can prove they all have the same inbox without trusting each other. If one mirror goes offline and later reconnects, it can efficiently determine exactly which objects it’s missing by comparing hashes or a Merkle tree, rather than re-syncing everything.

A possible evolution

I wouldn’t necessarily think of it as a “temporary area” that eventually disappears. Instead, I’d think of it as a distributed collaboration log that exists alongside the repository:

* Repository: immutable Git history protected by the integrity PIN.
* Collaboration log: immutable, signed PRs, comments, reviews, approvals, and other events, replicated across mirrors.
* Maintainer: the only actor that can promote a collaboration event into repository history by merging it.

That clean separation preserves the integrity guarantees of the repository while still allowing mirrors to accept, replicate, and preserve collaboration data whenever the authoritative repository node is offline. It also scales naturally if, in the future, you add issues, code reviews, CI results, or other collaborative features—they can all live in the same replicated collaboration layer without ever affecting the repository’s integrity until a maintainer explicitly incorporates changes into Git.
events.title: Update PRs on mirrors
